title: The Real IAF Heroes Who Inspired Netflix's Operation Safed Sagar
excerpt: The six-part series draws from the accounts of Air Chief Marshal B.S. Dhanoa and the late Squadron Leader Ajay Ahuja, whose sacrifice during the 1999 Kargil War is reaching global audiences for the first time.
body:
• Netflix's Operation Safed Sagar, which premiered August 7, is based on the real accounts of Air Chief Marshal B.S. Dhanoa and the late Squadron Leader Ajay Ahuja, who was killed during the 1999 Kargil War
  • Ahuja was shot down by a Stinger missile on May 27, 1999 while trying to locate a downed fellow pilot, and was posthumously awarded the Vir Chakra
  • The series was filmed at operational IAF bases with real MiG aircraft, and Dhanoa personally consulted on the project to ensure authenticity
  • Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said the production contributed over Rs 215 crore to the Indian economy, with Rs 49 crore going to VFX

The Men Behind the Characters

https://youtube.com/watch?v=kDKqpvo52nA

When Jimmy Shergill walks across a fictional air base as Wing Commander "Tony" Dhanoa in Netflix's Operation Safed Sagar, he is portraying a man who went on to become India's Chief of Air Staff. When Siddharth dons a flight suit as Squadron Leader Ajay Ahuja, he is stepping into the boots of a pilot who gave his life trying to save a fellow airman over the mountains of Kargil.

The six-episode series, which premiered on Netflix on August 7, is drawing attention not just for its aerial sequences and production values, but for the real military stories it brings to a global audience for the first time.

Ajay Ahuja: The Pilot Who Stayed Behind

On May 27, 1999, Squadron Leader Ajay Ahuja was on a photo reconnaissance mission over the Kargil sector when fellow pilot Flight Lieutenant K. Nachiketa's MiG-27 suffered an engine flame-out the previous day, forcing him to eject over enemy-held territory. Ahuja, serving as flight commander of the 17th Squadron — the Golden Arrows — chose to stay over hostile positions to guide a rescue helicopter toward the suspected crash site.

https://x.com/NetflixIndia/status/2085705087658172760

His MiG-21 was hit by a shoulder-fired FIM-92 Stinger missile. Ahuja's final radio transmission was stark: "Hercules, something has hit my plane, possibility of missile hit cannot be ruled out, I am ejecting." According to Indian Air Force data and post-mortem evidence, Ahuja ejected safely and landed alive but was killed on the ground. His body was recovered by soldiers of the 10th Battalion of the Garhwal Rifles. He was 31 years old.

On India's Independence Day that year, August 15, 1999, Squadron Leader Ajay Ahuja was posthumously awarded the Vir Chakra, one of India's highest gallantry honors.

B.S. Dhanoa: From Golden Arrows to Air Chief

Birender Singh Dhanoa commanded the Golden Arrows during the Kargil conflict and later rose to serve as India's Chief of Air Staff from 2016 to 2019. In 2019, on the 20th anniversary of the war, Dhanoa personally flew a MiG-21 in a "missing man" formation flyover at Air Force Station Bhisiana in Bhatinda to honor Ahuja and other fallen pilots — an aerial salute that leaves a deliberate gap in formation to mark the absence of a fallen comrade.

Dhanoa consulted extensively on the Netflix series, helping the production team recreate the operational realities of flying MiG-21s at extreme altitudes in the Kargil sector.

"India is ready to hear this story now. In fact, it is long overdue. Operation Safed Sagar deserves to be told, and I'm glad it is finally being brought to life."

— Air Chief Marshal (Retd.) B.S. Dhanoa

Dhanoa said his two wishes were for the IAF's Kargil story to reach a wide audience and for the series to inspire young Indians to join the Air Force. "Stories like these ignite young minds. Even today, after retirement, I keep telling veterans who served in wars to visit schools and share their experiences," he said.

A Martyr's Wife Speaks

At the trailer launch in Mumbai, attended by IAF veterans including Dhanoa and current Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh, one moment cut through the spectacle. Alka Ahuja, Squadron Leader Ajay Ahuja's widow, took the stage and said: "I don't have any videos of Ajay. At least, I have an image of Ajay now."

Siddharth, who portrays Ahuja, had tears in his eyes. "I didn't want to do injustice to somebody's memory," the actor said. "We ensured that we always stayed true to the integrity of a great man's memory and a soldier's story. Heroes don't look like heroes. They are heroes because of their actions."

Critical Response and Economic Impact

Early reviews have been largely favorable. NDTV gave the series 4 out of 5 stars, calling its pacing "perfect." The Indian Express praised the show for going "above and beyond, literally — it takes to the skies, showing us the Indian Air Force which pulled off a near-impossible feat, of striking from beyond the clouds through nerdy jugaad." Decider recommended streaming it as "a high-stakes military drama" that marries an entertaining fighter pilot narrative to real history.

The production's economic footprint has been substantial. Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said Operation Safed Sagar contributed over Rs 215 crore to the Indian economy, with Rs 49 crore going to visual effects. The series was filmed across operational IAF bases in Himachal Pradesh and at locations including the Shinku-La Pass, Jispa, Sissu, Rohtang, and the Drass Army base, with access to actual MiG aircraft and military infrastructure.

Why Diaspora Audiences Are Watching

For Indian diaspora viewers who remember the Kargil War as a defining moment from 1999, Operation Safed Sagar fills a gap. Previous Kargil-themed productions like LOC Kargil and Shershaah focused on Indian Army operations. This is the first major dramatization to center the Air Force's high-altitude campaign — the world's highest air operation — and with Netflix's reach across 190 countries, it puts a chapter of Indian military history on a global stage for the first time.
